content:
**Quick answer:** The best anti-inflammatory foods for arthritis are generally foods that fit within a healthy Mediterranean-style eating pattern: vegetables, fruit, beans, lentils, wholegrains, nuts, seeds, oily fish and unsaturated fats such as olive or rapeseed oil. No individual food can treat or cure arthritis, so diet should complement, not replace, medical care.

## What "anti-inflammatory food" actually means

The phrase is widely used online, and it can create unrealistic expectations. Inflammation is part of the body's immune response and is particularly important in inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis. Food should not be presented as medicine for arthritis.

A more useful way to think about anti-inflammatory eating is as a healthy overall dietary pattern containing plenty of plant foods, fibre and unsaturated fats. Think about your overall eating pattern rather than searching for one miracle ingredient.

## A Mediterranean-style pattern is the sensible starting point

A Mediterranean-style diet generally includes plenty of vegetables, fruit, beans and other pulses, wholegrains, nuts and seeds, fish, and olive oil or other unsaturated fats. The NHS discusses this type of eating pattern for people with rheumatoid arthritis while making clear there is no strong evidence that specific dietary changes alone improve the condition. View it as a healthy eating pattern, not a replacement for medication.

Focus on what you can add to meals, such as vegetables, pulses and wholegrains, rather than creating a long list of foods you are not allowed to eat.

## The building blocks

- Oily fish such as salmon, sardines, mackerel, trout, herring, pilchards and sprats provide long-chain omega-3 fats. The NHS recommends at least two portions of fish a week, including one portion of oily fish.
- Vegetables and fruit are the foundation. Aim for variety: leafy greens, broccoli, carrots, peppers, tomatoes, peas, berries, apples, pears and oranges. Frozen and canned count too; you do not need expensive berries or specialist powders.
- Beans, peas and lentils provide fibre, protein, vitamins and minerals, and slot into curries, soups, salads, stews and pasta dishes.
- Wholegrains and higher-fibre carbohydrates such as oats, wholegrain bread, wholewheat pasta, brown rice and potatoes with their skins. There is no need for most people with arthritis to eliminate carbohydrates.
- Nuts and seeds such as walnuts, almonds, flaxseed and pumpkin seeds provide fibre and unsaturated fats. Walnuts and flaxseed contain plant omega-3, which is not identical to the long-chain omega-3 in oily fish.
- Olive and rapeseed oil are unsaturated fats that fit the pattern. All fats are energy-dense, so oils are used in relatively small amounts; adding large quantities will not reduce arthritis pain.

## Turmeric, ginger and supplements: a word of caution

Turmeric, ginger, garlic and herbs can make meals flavourful and may help you rely less on salt, but claims about particular spices "fighting arthritis" are often much stronger than the evidence supports. Using them in ordinary cooking is different from taking concentrated supplements.

Be cautious with supplement marketing. Products marketed for inflammation, joint detox, cartilage rebuilding or rapid pain relief can make claims that go well beyond reliable evidence, and "natural" does not mean safe: natural products can still interact with medicines, cause side effects or be unsuitable for some health conditions. Speak to a pharmacist, GP or registered dietitian before starting a new supplement.

> **Food is not a substitute for treatment**
>
> This matters most for inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis. Diet should never be presented as an alternative to disease-modifying medication or other treatment recommended by your healthcare team. Do not stop, reduce or change prescribed medication because you have changed your diet.

## Nightshades, gluten, dairy and sugar

There is no universal list of foods that everybody with arthritis must avoid. There is no general NHS recommendation to remove nightshade vegetables (tomatoes, peppers, aubergines, potatoes) from your diet, and no reason to avoid gluten or dairy simply because you have arthritis; some people need to avoid particular foods because of diagnosed conditions, allergies or intolerances, which is different.

If you repeatedly notice that a particular food seems to affect your symptoms, keep a simple record and discuss it with a dietitian or healthcare professional rather than cutting out multiple food groups at once. An increasingly restrictive diet is not automatically a healthier or more anti-inflammatory one.

As for sugar, a diet high in sugary foods and drinks is not recommended for general health, but it is too simplistic to say one sugary food directly causes a flare or that removing sugar treats arthritis. Focus on the overall pattern rather than every teaspoon.

## Vegetarian and vegan eating

A plant-based eating pattern can include beans, chickpeas, lentils, tofu, vegetables, fruit, wholegrains, nuts, seeds, rapeseed oil and fortified dairy alternatives. People following restrictive vegan or vegetarian diets may need to pay particular attention to vitamin B12, iron, calcium, iodine and vitamin D. A registered dietitian can provide individual advice if needed.

## Weight, handled sensitively

Nobody should be blamed for arthritis because of their body weight. For people with osteoarthritis who are living with overweight or obesity, NICE states that weight loss can improve quality of life and physical function and reduce pain. Arthritis can itself make shopping, cooking and physical activity more difficult, so if weight management is appropriate for you, the support should be individual, kind and realistic.

## Building an arthritis-friendly plate

Seven simple changes to try: add an extra vegetable to your main meal; swap white bread or pasta for wholegrain sometimes; add lentils or beans to soups, stews and curries; choose fruit or unsalted nuts for some snacks; include fish regularly if it suits your diet; replace some saturated fats with unsaturated oils; and make changes gradually rather than chasing a perfect diet. Choose one change that feels manageable this week.

And if arthritis makes cooking difficult, convenience does not automatically mean unhealthy: frozen pre-cut vegetables, canned beans and lentils, frozen fruit, pre-cooked wholegrains, simple one-pan meals, sitting for food preparation, batch cooking on better days, or asking for help with chopping and heavy pans. An occupational therapist may also suggest equipment or ways of adapting kitchen tasks.

- Plenty of vegetables: broccoli, carrots, peppers, spinach, tomatoes, peas or others you enjoy.
- A source of protein: fish, beans, lentils, chickpeas, eggs or poultry.
- A higher-fibre carbohydrate: brown rice, wholegrain bread, wholewheat pasta or potatoes with their skins.
- A small amount of unsaturated fat: olive or rapeseed oil, for example.

## Key takeaways

- There is no single food or diet that cures arthritis; a Mediterranean-style eating pattern is a sensible approach.
- Vegetables, fruit, beans, lentils, wholegrains, nuts and seeds form the foundation; oily fish provides long-chain omega-3 fats.
- There is usually no need to eliminate nightshade vegetables, gluten or dairy simply because you have arthritis.
- Be cautious about supplement and superfood claims.
- Diet does not replace medical treatment, and medication should never be changed because of a dietary change.

## Frequently asked questions

### What foods reduce arthritis inflammation quickly?

No food has been shown to reliably and quickly switch off arthritis inflammation. Be cautious of products or diets promising rapid results.

### Is salmon good for arthritis?

Salmon is an oily fish and provides long-chain omega-3 fatty acids. It can be a nutritious part of a balanced diet, but it should not be described as a treatment for arthritis.

### Should people with arthritis avoid tomatoes?

There is no general recommendation that everyone with arthritis should avoid tomatoes or other nightshade vegetables.

### Are turmeric supplements good for arthritis?

Do not assume concentrated turmeric or other herbal supplements are safe or effective because they are natural. Speak to a pharmacist, GP or dietitian before starting one.

## A gentle next step

Healthy eating with arthritis does not have to mean a restrictive diet or expensive anti-inflammatory products. A varied, balanced approach built around ordinary nutritious foods is a more realistic place to start. If you have a medical condition, take regular medication, have experienced unexplained weight loss or plan major dietary changes, speak to your GP, pharmacist or a registered dietitian. You can also explore practical arthritis information and support from Living With Arthritis.
